page.text:
While groups formalize symmetries through a single invertible operation, the
richness of classical arithmetic and geometry requires the simultaneous presence
of two interacting operations: addition and multiplication.

A *ring* unites these operations: addition forms an abelian group (permitting
arbitrary translations and subtractions), multiplication forms a monoid
(providing composition and an identity), and the two operations are bound
together by the *distributive laws*:
$$ a \cdot (b + c) = a \cdot b + a \cdot c \quad \text{and} \quad (a + b) \cdot c = a \cdot c + b \cdot c. $$
The distributive property ensures that multiplication behaves as an endomorphism
of the additive group. Conceived through the pioneering work of Richard Dedekind,
David Hilbert, and Emmy Noether, rings provide the overarching framework for
integers, polynomials, matrices, and algebraic functions.
